h1: SEO consultant vs SEO agency: who actually does the work?
metaTitle: SEO Consultant vs Agency: Who Does the Work?
metaDescription: SEO consultant vs SEO agency is a question of who executes. A consultant sells judgement. Here are the four in-house roles you need before hiring one.
answer: A consultant sells judgement: an audit, a roadmap, a monthly call. An agency sells judgement plus the hands that execute it. Indian consultants charge ₹15,000–₹60,000 a day or ₹25,000–₹1,00,000 a month for advisory. That only pays off if you already employ a writer, a developer and someone who owns the roadmap.
takeaways: The difference isn't quality or seniority. It's **who publishes the page**. A consultant tells you the page should exist.
Four things must already be in your building: a writer who ships, a developer with reserved hours, a marketer who owns the roadmap, and a release cadence that actually deploys.
A good audit generates 100–150 tickets. In a product backlog with none of them owned by name, roughly two will ship.
A consultant is often the **right first purchase** and the wrong second one. Buy the judgement, then decide who executes it.

body: Both a consultant and an agency will tell you your category pages are thin, your internal linking is accidental and you've been cannibalising two of your own money pages for eighteen months. The good ones will tell you in the same first fortnight, and roughly the same way.
Then one of them writes the pages and the other one waits to hear whether you did.

That's the entire distinction, and it's worth being blunt about because the pitch decks blur it. Consultants aren't more strategic than agencies. Agencies aren't less experienced than consultants — the best consultants usually ran agency teams first. The variable is execution capacity, and it's the variable that decides whether anything happens.

callout.title: The question that settles it
callout.body: "Who writes the page?" Ask it in the first call. If the answer is "we'll brief your team", you're buying a consultant, whatever the invoice says. That's fine — as long as your team exists.

sections.h2: The four in-house roles a consultant depends on
body: A consultant is a multiplier on an execution capability you already have. Multiply zero by anything and you still have nothing, which is how ₹3 lakh audits end up as PDFs in a Drive folder nobody has opened since March.
Before you sign, check that all four of these exist. Not "we could probably find someone" — exist, with a name attached.
numbered: **A writer who ships.** Someone who turns a brief into a published page every week without a purchase order, a procurement cycle or a three-person review chain. Not a founder who'll "try to get to it this weekend". They won't.

**A developer with reserved hours.** Not "we have an engineering team". Ring-fenced hours, monthly, that don't get eaten by the release. Four to twelve hours a month covers most SEO implementation work; zero covers none of it.

**A marketer who owns the roadmap.** Someone whose performance review contains the organic number, who will chase ticket 37 into a sprint and take the argument to the product manager. Without this person, every recommendation is optional, and optional work doesn't ship.

**A release cadence that actually deploys.** Weekly or fortnightly. If your site ships quarterly, a consultant's roadmap ages out before it lands, and you'll pay them again in six months to re-audit a site that never changed.

callout.title: Three out of four isn't a pass
callout.body: Miss any one and the whole thing stalls. The most common miss is the third — everyone has a marketer, almost nobody has a marketer whose bonus depends on organic. That's the role that turns a recommendation into a shipped page.

body: Consultant pricing isn't priced on hours, whatever the invoice says. It's priced on the cost of the decision you're about to get wrong. A replatform that drops 40% of your organic traffic costs more than any day rate on this list, which is why the day rates look high next to a junior agency retainer and are usually good value anyway.
The bands you'll meet in India:
bullets: **₹15,000–₹60,000 a day.** Lower end for a competent specialist, upper end for someone with a public reputation and a decade of migrations behind them.
**₹25,000–₹1,00,000 a month** for advisory — two to five days, a standing call, and Slack or WhatsApp access between them.
**₹75,000–₹2,00,000 a month** for a fractional SEO lead at one to two days a week. Different product: they attend your stand-ups, own the roadmap, and manage your agency or freelancers.
**₹50,000–₹3,00,000** for a one-off audit and roadmap, depending on site size and whether you get a working session afterwards or just a document.
**₹3,000–₹10,000 an hour** for ad hoc calls — the cheapest sanity check available before you sign anything else. [How SEO gets priced](/cost/seo-pricing-models) covers the models in full.

sections.h2: How a good audit dies in a backlog
body: This is the failure mode, and it almost never looks like a failure while it's happening.

You commission a ₹2 lakh audit. It's excellent — 60 pages, genuinely diagnostic, 140 findings ranked by impact. The consultant walks the team through it, everyone agrees it's sharp, and the tickets go into Jira.

There they sit behind a checkout bug, a payments integration and the Q3 product roadmap. Nobody on the sprint team has organic traffic in their objectives. Two tickets ship in three months, both cosmetic. In month four somebody asks what happened to that SEO thing, and the consultant looks expensive.

The consultant was fine. The pipe was blocked. And here's the bit an agency should admit too: **we have the same problem with anything needing your engineers**. What an agency bypasses is everything living in the CMS — content, on-page, internal linking, metadata, most schema — which is the majority of a typical audit. What it can't bypass is your deploy queue.
bullets: **Before commissioning an audit, name the owner of ticket 37.** Out loud, in the room. If nobody volunteers, buy execution instead of advice.
**Ask for ten findings, not a hundred.** A ranked ten that ship beat a hundred that don't, and a good consultant will happily give you the ten.
**Put implementation hours in the same purchase order** as the audit. Separate budgets are how the second half never gets approved.

**Re-audit only after you've shipped.** Paying twice to be told the same thing is the most common waste in this category. [What an audit should actually find](/journal/what-an-seo-audit-should-actually-find) sets the bar for the first one.

sections.h2: When to move from consultant to retainer
body: A consultant is often the right first purchase — buy the judgement cheaply, find out whether the problem is strategy or capacity, then decide. Four signals tell you the answer is capacity.
bullets: **The same recommendation appears in three consecutive monthly calls, unactioned.** You're paying ₹50,000 a month to be reminded of something you can't do.
**Your writer is the bottleneck.** One in-house writer produces two to four decent pages a month. If the roadmap needs twelve, no amount of advice closes the gap.
**You need links.** No consultant runs outreach at volume — it's a full-time operation with its own headcount. This is the cleanest reason to switch.
**The roadmap owner left.** The moment the person who chased tickets resigns, an advisory retainer becomes a subscription to unread documents. Cancel it or replace them the same month.

callout.title: Both, deliberately
callout.body: A fractional lead at ₹1,00,000/mo plus an agency at ₹75,000/mo is a defensible ₹21 lakh a year — the lead owns internal politics and the roadmap, the agency owns capacity. It only works if the lead's review includes the agency's output rather than competing with it. We run [SEO from ₹75,000/mo](/pricing) inside exactly that arrangement often enough to recommend it.

body: If all four in-house roles genuinely exist — a writer who ships weekly, a developer with reserved hours, a marketer whose review contains the organic number, and a deploy cadence measured in weeks — hire the consultant. A ₹50,000/month advisory retainer buys you the best judgement available and doesn't duplicate people you're already paying. Anything else is waste.

If any one of the four is missing, hire the agency. The consultant's roadmap will be correct and it will sit in a backlog, and you'll have spent ₹6 lakh a year on a document. At ₹75,000/month an agency ships the CMS-side majority of that roadmap without touching your sprint, which is the difference between a plan and a result.

And if you're not sure which of the four you're missing, that's the cheapest question in this category: buy three hours of a consultant's time at ₹3,000–₹10,000 an hour and ask. A good one will tell you to hire someone else, which is how you know they're worth the day rate. [What SEO consulting covers](/services/seo-consulting) is where we'd start.

One thing neither model should ever offer you: a promised ranking position. Nobody controls Google's index. What we commit to is movement against your own frozen baseline — your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic, measured in your CRM, beaten inside 90 days or we keep working free until it is.

versus.verdict: If you already have a writer who ships weekly, a developer with reserved hours and a marketer whose review contains the organic number, a ₹50,000/month consultant is the better buy — miss any one of those and the roadmap dies in a backlog, and a ₹75,000/month agency is the cheaper way to get it shipped.

faqs.q: What does an SEO consultant actually do?
faqs.a: Audits, prioritisation, roadmaps, migration planning, penalty diagnosis, settling internal arguments about what to build next, and often helping you hire. What they don't do is write the content, run outreach or push the code. That's the whole distinction from an agency.

faqs.q: What do SEO consultants charge in India?
faqs.a: ₹15,000–₹60,000 a day, ₹25,000–₹1,00,000 a month for advisory of two to five days, and ₹75,000–₹2,00,000 a month for a fractional lead at one to two days a week. A standalone audit and roadmap runs ₹50,000–₹3,00,000 depending on site size.

faqs.q: Do I need a consultant or an agency?
faqs.a: Count your in-house roles. A writer who publishes weekly, a developer with reserved hours, a marketer who owns the organic number, and a weekly or fortnightly deploy cadence. All four present, hire a consultant. Any one missing, hire an agency — the advice will otherwise sit unactioned.

faqs.q: Why do SEO audits never get implemented?
faqs.a: Because 140 findings enter a product backlog behind a checkout bug and a payments integration, and nobody on the sprint team has organic traffic in their objectives. The fix is naming an owner before you commission the audit and asking for a ranked ten rather than an exhaustive hundred.

faqs.q: Is a fractional SEO lead the same as a consultant?
faqs.a: Different product. A consultant advises from outside on a defined scope. A fractional lead sits inside — attends stand-ups, owns the roadmap, manages your agency or freelancers, and is accountable for the number. Expect ₹75,000–₹2,00,000 a month for one to two days a week.
